title: Sand
strapline: One material, two personalities — dry sand pours like water, wet sand holds every idea you press into it.
intent: Discover that the same material behaves in two completely different ways: dry sand flows, trickles and escapes; wet sand moulds, packs and holds a shape.
Explore capacity and quantity hands-on — filling, emptying, heaping, levelling — long before anyone says the word 'volume'.
Build pouring, scooping and sieving control, from two-handed bucket tipping to careful funnel work.
Investigate cause and effect with sieves, wheels, funnels and tubes — what falls through, what gets caught, what makes the wheel spin.
Use sand as a first mark-making surface — fingers, sticks and combs leave trails that can be smoothed away and tried again.
Bury, hide and find — the deep satisfaction of things disappearing and coming back.
implementation: Offer dry and damp sand in the same week (or the same tray, half and half) and let children discover the difference before you name it.
Narrate the physics in everyday words: 'it's trickling through your fingers', 'the wet sand is sticking together', 'the sieve caught the shells but the sand fell through'.
Model the sandcastle craft honestly — pack it down, tap the bucket, lift slowly — and let children meet the failure of dry-sand castles for themselves before offering the water.
Ask capacity questions at the point of pouring: nearly full, half full, room for more, too heavy to lift?
Bury objects for finding — and let children set up hunts for each other, which brings counting and describing for free.
Kneel at baby level with treasure to press and trails to copy — sand is a whole-body, all-ages material.
Keep tools sparse some days: just hands and sand slows the play down and deepens it.
key_questions: Why won't this castle stay up — what does it need?
What do you think will fall through the sieve, and what will get stuck?
How many scoops will fill your bucket? Shall we count?
Where has all the sand gone — can you find it?
How does the dry sand feel different from the wet sand?
What could you use to get the sand up to the top?

impact.text: Babies and toddlers plunge hands into sand, letting it fall through their fingers and enjoying the feel of it.
Children fill, empty, heap, bury and rediscover — buckets, moulds and hidden treasure — returning to the same schemas again and again.
Children pour dry sand through funnels and sieves with growing control, adjusting their tipping when it overflows.
Children investigate the sand tools as mechanisms — turning the wheel, testing which sieve lets shells through — working out how each one works.
Children notice that wet sand holds a shape and dry sand collapses, ask why the castle fell, and add water on purpose to change it.
Children use comparative and capacity language as they work: full, nearly empty, heavier, too much.
Children draw trails, comb repeating patterns and make prints in smoothed sand, noticing the marks they leave.
Children try out the describing words offered to them — trickle, gritty, damp, crumbly — in their own sand talk.

enhancements: A jug of water and small watering cans beside dry sand — the single best provocation: children engineer the change themselves.
Sieves of different gauges with a shell-and-pebble mix, so sorting happens mechanically and sparks 'why' talk.
Sand combs, rakes and pattern cards for large-scale mark-making and repeating patterns.
Buried 'fossils' or letter pebbles with brushes — archaeologist play that slows hands right down.
Balance scales at the sand tray — is a cup of wet sand heavier than a cup of dry?
Ramps, guttering and tubes clamped to the tray edge for pouring sand downhill into targets.
Tiny-world add-ins — diggers, dinosaurs, arctic animals — to shift the tray into story territory for a week.

playing_exploring: Children find things out with their hands and whole bodies — plunging, burying, tipping — before any adult explains a thing.
Babies explore sand purely through the senses; older children turn the same tray into building sites and beaches.
active_learning: Rebuilding a collapsed castle, and getting it to stand the third time, is persistence with a visible reward.
Children keep refining their pour — slower, closer, smaller scoop — until the funnel stops overflowing.
creating_thinking: Children form real theories — 'it needs water to stick' — and test them immediately.
They invent their own problems to solve: a moat that keeps emptying, a tunnel that keeps caving in.
